prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I moved from my opening first choice, aberration-corrected electron optics (B001), to the optical lattice clock after reading the opening ballots. The criterion I apply is the one I use in public: a discovery or invention, not lifetime achievement, with an identifiable topic and identifiable people. B024 meets it cleanly. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a single original idea, and the performance gain is quantitative and checkable: fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, reproduced in several laboratories and checked by international clock comparisons. Ye's group carried the platform to record accuracy and stability, so the credit divides naturally between proposal and realization at two names. The consequences are concrete: the roadmap for redefining the second, tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. Four colleagues ranked it first and five members placed it in their top three, myself included, a spread that is notable on a shortlist where most candidates have disputed credit or incomplete maturity. Support alone is not merit, but here the independent merit arguments from colleagues who know the field (Lindroth, Kroll, Johansson) agree with what I can judge from outside atomic physics: a clear invention with a measurable, replicated result.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The 2005 prize covered the optical frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions, and optical clocks sit on top of both. A committee could read B024 as the third prize in one lineage. The redefinition of the second has also not happened, so the practical impact is still prospective. My own microscopy-based worry is that I am ranking outside my field and leaning on colleagues' technical judgment about the proposal-versus-demonstration chronology and the roles of other groups (Lemonde, Hollberg, the ion-clock community). If that chronology turned out to favour a different pair, the configuration would need rework.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the lattice clock first because the two-person credit is clean and the 2005 comb prize makes this a natural, timely successor rather than a premature choice.
responses.response: I agree on the allocation and largely on timing, and this is what moved me. I would not call it a pure successor, though. The comb and ion-clock prizes are enabling technology for the lattice clock, but the magic-wavelength idea is a distinct invention, and the citation should say so to avoid the impression of repetition. I also note that Johansson ranked circuit QED second and disclosed Chalmers and WACQT ties. That is his to manage; for my part I would not treat his disclosure as a reason to discount his merit view of B043, and I do not carry it into B024.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B024 only seventh, noting that Hall's comb prize and Wineland's ion-clock prize create overlap, and that credit for the first demonstration versus the proposal may be disputed between Katori, Ye and others.
responses.response: This is the most serious qualification on my preferred choice and I do not want to wave it away. My answer is that overlap with enabling prizes is a framing problem rather than a disqualifier: the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a frequency ruler, while the lattice clock rewards a new trapping scheme that removes Doppler, recoil and Stark shifts while keeping many atoms. I accept his point that the chronology of the first demonstration needs checking before the citation is fixed; if Ye's role is better described as realizing the best-performing system than as co-inventing, the citation wording should reflect that, though a two-name prize remains defensible. He ranks it only seventh, well below his statistical-physics and 2D-materials picks, and I respect that difference in weighting; I would ask him whether his concern is about the novelty of the lineage or only about the credit chronology.

responses.point: Danielsson puts twisted bilayer graphene (B003) first as a clear, original discovery of new phases of matter, now confirmed independently by many groups with ripe timing, and notes that the first-author experimentalist is missing from the credit.
responses.response: I agree B003 is the strongest condensed-matter case and I keep it as my first alternative. I place it just behind B024 for two reasons. First, the credit problem is real: Cao and the early-career experimental leaders, and Dean, Young and Yazdani on the broader moire programme, sit outside a three-name limit, and I do not think we can wave this away because the theory-experiment pairing looks tidy. Second, the pairing mechanism and sample-dependence are unsettled, which Eriksson, Kroll and Mehlig each flagged. I would not call it premature, since the flat-band prediction and the 2018 observation are secure, but it has less settled interpretation than the clock. If the committee wants a condensed-matter prize this year, I would support B003 with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, though my opening list had only the first two.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks Car-Parrinello ab initio molecular dynamics (B058) first as an original method that reshaped computational materials physics, while acknowledging the committee may be reluctant to honour a simulation tool.
responses.response: I sympathise with the substance, since first-principles dynamics is also what I rely on when interpreting interface structure measured in the microscope. But it was ranked by only two members, and the question he raises is the right one: is it a discovery or invention in physics, or a method whose home is chemistry, given the 1998 chemistry prize for density-functional theory? The credit is the cleanest on the list, which counts in its favour. I would not put it in my configuration this year, but my own opening candidate was also a tool, so I cannot argue against instrument-type prizes on principle. I would say instead that tools qualify when, as with the lattice clock, the invention makes a new class of measurement possible and not only a faster one.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's contribution is best credited as co-invention or as realization to record accuracy, which the citation wording depends on.
Whether the committee reads B024 as a third prize in the comb and ion-clock lineage after 2005 and 2012.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as a prerequisite for recognition.

Whether my own B001 remains a serious alternative given only one first-place ranking and the instrumentation concern; I cannot resolve the boundary with the STEM corrector line from the supplied credit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal conflict is apparent from my profile for B024, B003 or the other shortlisted candidates. I flag two general points. First, my profile lists long-running academic exchanges with Japanese universities, including a University of Tokyo fellowship, and one credited name in B024 is based in Japan; no personal or collaborative relationship is documented, but this should be checked if the committee wishes. Second, I rank B001 as an alternative and am a professional user of aberration-corrected TEM, a field-level interest rather than a tie to Rose, Urban or Haider. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers, which affects only the committee composition, not any candidate.
